I took care of my dying mother and stopped my university education for it. My sister also helped a lot and went part time during that time. My brother? He didn’t do a thing because his starting career was more important to him. I never really got back on track in university because these four years were just so straining and hard that I was caught in a deep depression after my mother had died. My sister never went back to full time work. My brother has a big career.
Now - nearly 20 years later - my mother in law slowly shows the first signs of illness and my partner told me that he assumes that I will help taking care of her. And I was „No!“ She has four sons. First it is THEIR duty to take care of her or organize someone professional who does this job. I did my part. I refuse to take care of her. He was shocked, but he simply has no clue. And I am so mad that in his mind it is completely normal that their wives have to do the caring…
And when I am about to die or am lucky enough to get so old that I cannot take care of myself the last thing I would do to my daughter is to let her take care of me and destroying her life doing it.

Cared for my mother for near 10 years, full time, on my own.
It’s difficult to do anything for yourself in the declining years because it’s 24/7 x 52 weeks..
This is under appreciated , even by other family members.
Loss in earnings, savings, supper, relationships, friends, vocation, hobbies, sports or adventure activities…. Loss of fitness and energy, increase in weight..
Whatever you do the house Smells like old people, so you become.. reluctant to invite people over.
Social isolation just happens, might not talk to a sensible person in days,
Find yourself rambling on to cashiers while mums in the car, in the parking lot and you hope she hasn’t done a runner!
I was told that I had enjoyed a 10 year vacation, cost free…
I will never forget that comment.

There was a lady in my hometown out in the country who would take care of two or three old people in their homes, so obviously this wasn't full-time, but she would check on them several times a day, and when they died, they left their homes to her. When I was in college, I rented from a childless lady whose niece would come by and check on her, and my landlady said when she died, that niece would get everything. So as my landlady's body broke down, years after I moved out, I assume that niece took over her full care.

It's sad that the last few years of your life could be the most frightening years of your life because you're in a terrible nursing home, or you're alone and falling down and no one's checking on you. But through your county, or maybe a larger neighboring county, there should be help for you. You just need to do the research while you still have your mental capacity, and line things up. And when I say you, I mean me.

snippet.textDisplay:
As someone reaching this stage of being elderly and noticing the decline, I don't want to be burdensome. My kids are already so busy and it just wouldn't be fair to put my care on them like that.
In a more natural state of being, the decline and the end wouldn't take so long, but end of life has been extended beyond what it used to be, and that's not always a good thing for anyone!

It is beyond hard for a loving child to deal with all of that, as well as the pressures of their spouse and children, and often work too. This is an excellent video which hopefully will help release the guilt for so many. I've had my life, and my children don't deserve the added strain on their already over- busy, over- stressful lives. Once the caring reaches beyond loving care to medical care, then it isn't wrong to hand that care over to the professionals. That way, you can come visit and enjoy your time with your loved one, dignity intact all round. ❤

snippet.textDisplay: All I can say is they CAN be overruled, and should be. Forget the security cameras, just get her admitted whether she likes it or not. My sister and I spent months trying to persuade my mother to go into a rest home, which thankfully in NZ is paid for by the state. She absolutely refused. After one particularly big argument she caved in & the irony is that she was very happy there. Rest homes always have something going on, they bring a tea trolley around, there's occasional entertainment and caregivers are always popping in & out. The care wasn't perfect but as I lived close by I was able to take her out a couple of times a week, have her at my place in front of the fire with the dog on her lap etc. That went on for years. In the end she did get both cantankerous and incontinent and I realised I could simply never have managed her on my own. I don't think any single person or couple can. It takes a team & rest homes have the staff, even if it's not as many as they should. The last couple of years were not pretty but I feel it was the only real option. So you guys need to make the decision now & do it against her will. All of you will be happier for it, including her.

snippet.textDisplay:
@patpeifer7871 If it's any consolation, I was in the same position. Even to considering cameras as Mum was letting strangers into the house. Mum lived 9hrs from me, refused to move closer, and wanted me to move up there to look after her. I said no, my job, life and my children's lives were back at home. She wasn't socialising with anyone and at 88 she wasn't doing anything, but she still refused to move, or accept help from anyone else but me and my children . Eventually, life takes its natural course. After 2 years of having to travel up every time she fell (about every 5 weeks), stay up there 2 weeks to get her and the house clean again, get her well fed, set up daily carers that she'd Cancel as soon as I'd gone...she eventually had a more serious fall. This time, during Covid, after an 8hr wait for an ambulance whilst I travelled up (a neighbour was with her) they wouldn't take her to hospital. After staying a week being woken up several times a night to get on her the commode with my son ( who had also taken time off work to help me look after her) and realising she couldn't be left alone this time - I called her doctor in who convinced her she needed respite care. After that, things fell into place. The dementia she'd been assessed with but denied actually helped her deal with the process in the end. It was difficult getting her down to my home town, an expensive ambulance was hired. And sorting her house to get it sold, then selling and emptying it was a nightmare from such a distance, but she's safe and well looked after now. However, that 2 years of constant stress, travelling, looking after her to the point of exhaustion and pain (I had arthritis, now severe) broke my health, and I had to give up my job. I'd advise you to be firm with her. A health professional told her she was being selfish but she refused to accept it. My children, who have always adored her, feel resentful sometimes (then guilty for feeling that) because of the impact it had on me.
Mum is still alive, existing as a non comprehending, non communicating, doubly incontinent shell. They're in denial, thinking they'll stay active and then one night just die peacefully in their sleep. People live longer now, but the last years aren't in good health. As a loving daughter you think you should do it all, you want to accommodate all their wishes. Maybe you can, but the odds are you won't be able to. Showing her this video might be a step too far but you need to point out the reality, before it breaks you and possibly the relationships surrounding.

snippet.textDisplay: I am 53 years old now. My mom is going to be 78 tomorrow!  I quit my job in 2020 as a hygienist due to severe cervical & lumbar spinal stenosis. In 2022 my mom had a stroke. That was the worst thing that could of happened. I am not married and i hace 2 sisters who are.. one was living at home till my mom had her stroke. She & her husband inherited his grandmoms house so they left my moms. My mom really needed the help. After my mom got home from the hospital and rehabilitation things were really bad with my sisters and myself. Everyone was angry and there was no trust. My sister and her husband both beat me up in their home because my sister took my moms trust and i wanted it to read at my house. They literally tackled me and i had no car and had to call the police. My other sister also went bonkers and attacked me for telling her to go away .. my mom didnt want her in the house. Both sisters came at me and they filed a PFA on me! I am disabled and  would never go after anyone. The next year my mom had her cat bite her and sent her to the ER.. had a bad infection.. it was a terrible 2024. I am my mom POA… and i am exhausted. After 5 years of caring for my mom and not myself .. my spine has gotten so much worse. It didnt help that my sisters attacked me and the husband. I am so fed up with everything & everyone. My mom is home now bedridden with a live in caretaker but i do all her bills and buy her food . I was hoping that when i first went out on disability that i could strengthen myself to go back to work. I am worse now then i was 5 years ago. Caring for my mom and having to deal with my crazy sisters is going to be the end of me. I can not afford to be on SSDI and pay my bills anymore and need to work PT. Now i am in such a bad state with extreme anxiety & fatigue. I should be getting neck surgery but now i cant even do that. I give up.. i feel like my mom has killed me and do not know how i am going to survive now.

snippet.textDisplay: My 86 narcissistic father-in-law just died 2 weeks ago. He had Parkinson's and he was wretched by the time he died. He did not want to go into a nursing home and my mother-in-law wanted to keep him home. He was in and out of a hospital and rehab the last 6 weeks of his life but other than that he was home. Having to help my husband and my mother-in-law take care of him the past few years has really changed my mind about nursing homes. I know people don't always get the best care in them but people taking care of elderly in the last few years of their lives are under so much stress. I never wanted to go into a nursing home but after going through this with my father-in-law, I told my kids you put me into a nursing home and go live your life. I would rather myself suffer in a nursing home than to put my kids through this stress for several years before I die.

snippet.textDisplay:
This is so on the mark. The last twelve months were some of the hardest of my life. I am 67, drawing my state pension but still having to work full time (although I work at home) and a year ago today (12th April 2024) my mum had a bad fall (this was the third, that I know of, she hadn't told me about the previous ones). She fell in the bathroom and couldn't get up. My partner and I couldn't move her and it took him and the two ambulance staff to get her into a wheelchair. She spent 3 1/2 months in hospital, ending up doubly incontinent, bed bound and completely dependent on others. There was no way she could return to her own home so she came to live with me. It was ok at first, but there had been signs when she was in hospital that all was not well and some of her behaviour was extremely difficult to deal with (we now know she has Lewy body dementia). There was just me to look after her (my partner and don't live together and he had to be away for three months), with two carers coming in four times daily for a maximum of two hours in total. I couldn't move her or turn her, or change her on my own (because she couldn't help me and it needed two people) although I did my best. I found some of the things she did so disgusting that I found myself trying to avoid going into the room - or hoping she would be asleep when I did have to go in. There was no-one to sit with her while I took the washing to be dried (I don't have space for a dryer so was using my partner's), nor when I went shopping, so I had to leave her alone at those times and I couldn't always drop what I was doing to see what she wanted when she called me, which made me feel guilty and sometimes angry too because so much was expected of me. When I did have to go out I had to be back in time to let the carers in because giving them keys or access would have caused problems with my contents insurance. There were also people turning up at odd times to do reviews on her and never with an appointment (only one appointment was made and the doctors gave the District Nurse the wrong time so she was an hour early. I had one DN turn up unannounced at 3pm on a Sunday afternoon (I was collecting the washing and had to rush back). In the end it became too much for me. She slept much of the day and then, of course, couldn't sleep at night. I was so tired, and I lost count of the nights I cried myself to sleep. My cousin rang me and said she could tell from my voice that I was cracking under the strain because I just didn't sound like me any more. I was beginning to resent mum being there, which made me feel even more guilty and wasn't how I'd envisaged what would be her final months, and I was in a downward spiral. On 7th January she moved into a care home, where she is receiving nursing care because of her needs. They are surprised I managed for as long as I did because they are trained professionals and they find her challenging. She wants to go home and can't understand why she can't but she isn't safe to be on her own. It's the last thing either of us wanted but in the end there was no other way. I go over twice a week to see her, and it can be difficult, but with the distance between us and my knowing that other people who understand her needs better than I could are responsible for her well-being, my love for her that I was in danger of losing has returned. It's like she is two people though, my mum and a stranger that I don't know and who I wish would just get out of her body and leave us both alone.

All I can say to anyone faced with looking after a loved one like this is that it's not for everyone, and if it's not for you please don't do it, let the professionals do it and don't feel guilty about that. I love my mum, and I looked after her for five months, but it nearly destroyed me. You have to recognise when you can't go on and accept it.

snippet.textDisplay:
I completely agree. It is possible to live independently and stay mentally and physically strong well into our 80s and 90s. I’ve seen it too, and it’s incredibly inspiring.
At the same time, I also know that sometimes people face things way outside of their control—health conditions, injuries, or systemic issues that don’t come from lifestyle choices alone. So I never want to be judgmental about what aging ‘should’ look like.
But you’re absolutely right. There’s power in personal responsibility, and I do believe we have more influence over our long-term health than many of us realize. Thank you for bringing this perspective into the conversation. It’s such an important one.

Caregiving is brutal. I dont doubt it will take 3 years to completely restore my health.

snippet.textDisplay:
I feel the same way when I listen to stories about wayward adult children who are always in financial need, want to move back home, and worse, are emotionally and financially draining drug addicts, alcoholics, or have a criminal nature that zeros in on their parent's finances. Why should parents pay for their kid's college? Their weddings? Be an on-call babysitter? It works both ways.

In general, all adults aged 18+ must adopt a lifestyle to make themselves as independent as possible. I speak as an adult child and one who works in healthcare and have witnessed some wicked disregard for the elderly from various people, i.e., the public at large, the government, their healthcare providers, and their family members. Yet after their death, everybody wants a piece of what is left, especially the government and the family.

This is not a simple black-and-white issue. It is a swirling cloud of endless gray. EVERYONE is one accident or unexpected life-altering diagnosis away from losing their health and independence and financial ruin. 

The advice in this video is sound and necessary and will work well for some families. Unfortunately, life is complex and messy, and most scenarios will require a lot more finesse to work well for both sides. One thing NEVER to do is abandon your elderly loved one in a facility. You need to check in on their care regularly. You need to be heard from and seen by staff. Even people with dementia feel physical pain and should not be left soiled and unkempt. Adult children may not be doing DIRECT care, but they still need to be part of their parent's life and death with dignity.

snippet.textDisplay: I am sure that many of us faced a decision that what is my purpose! I made a choice to quit work to look after my mom. I have no regrets. Her worst in dementia was during Co>I'd. We, as brothers and sisters, would not let her go to a nursing home. I thank God I was able to move in with her and my sister, too, she too, had to quit her job, and we both took care of her needs. My mother got so angry at times that she couldn't look after herself. My mother resented every minute, but yet she was so grateful that she was not alone. For those who are facing this, I encourage you to pray that God will give you strength.

snippet.textDisplay: I’ve spent all day beating myself up because I don’t have a job and I am on my own at the age of 60. My mums funeral is in 2 days. I spent the last 3 years of my life caring for her and my dad. I may continue to care for my dad , but im broken. My life is shattered. My daughter has turned against me, stopped me seeing my granddaughter. My brother let me take the bulk of the responsibility, while he carried on with his life, his wife did nothing. Didn’t even contact me when mum died, said she was busy supporting my brother. Ive realised, from watching this video, that i dont have to beat myself up. I did right by my mum, and my dad. He wont go into a home, unless it’s forced on him, and i do think that is selfish. I do know i see my family differently now, and i should hold my head up high. My daughter should be ashamed of herself, not me. Caring for elderly parents is really hard, and having family that attack you and refuse to help is not unusual. My family have shocked me and demoralised me. Thank you for posting this video.
